title: Post-Fire Response of Miilux 450 Wear-Resistant Steel Under Different Cooling Methods
abstract: Abstract The post-fire performance of Miilux 450 wear-resistant steel has been examined in detail. Three cooling methods including air cooling (AC), water cooling (WC), and CO₂ fire extinguisher cooling (CFE), were employed after the samples had been exposed to elevated temperatures ranging from 400 °C to 1000 °C. Next, tensile tests were carried out on the samples to determine the key mechanical parameters, specifically the yield strength and ultimate tensile strength. The findings showed that yield and ultimate tensile strengths decreased by up to 60% and 55%, respectively, up to 700 °C, and only minor differences among cooling methods were detected up to 700 °C. Above 700 °C, WC notably increased the strength and hardness compared to AC and CFE, which is attributable to martensitic transformation, though at the expense of ductility. The modulus of elasticity exhibited minimal reduction (< 12%) until 1000 °C and cooling methods thus have almost no effect on the modulus of elasticity. On the other hand, hardness trends paralleled strength variations. These changes were explained in terms of microstructural alterations that occurred due to the heat treatments employed. Predictive equations have been proposed to estimate post-fire mechanical properties as a function of temperature and the cooling method.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Traditional structural mild steel materials have been extensively employed in a wide variety of applications for a long time due to their good ductility, weldability and cost effectiveness. However, steels with higher properties have begun to be produced as a result of increasing architectural requirements, the need for light-weight structures and the necessity for materials that can withstand harsher conditions. Additionally, advances in steel making and welding techniques have enabled steel manufacturers to offer higher performance steels to the market [ 1 ,  2 ]. Based on yield strength (σy), structural steels are commonly classified as mild steels (σy ≤ 460 MPa), high-strength steels (HSS, 460 < σy < 960 MPa), and ultra-high-strength steels (UHSS, σy ≥ 960 MPa) [ 3 ].

Since conventional mild and high strength steels are widely employed in civil engineering applications, their behavior under extreme conditions such as fire has been studied in detail. Outinen and Makelainen [ 3 ] and Outinen and Makelainen [ 4 ] investigated the effect of high temperature on two different conventional carbon steel grades i.e., S355 and S460. Lee et al. [ 5 ] examined the condition of ASTM A992 steel under the influence of high temperature by considering three different cooling methods. Their studies showed that there is a small change in the yield strength value up to 700 °C. Lu et al. [ 6 ] studied the mechanical properties of Q235, Q345, and Q420 steel grades exposed to fire. Their findings revealed that changes in mechanical behavior begin to occur at temperatures above 700 °C. Zeybek et al. [ 7 ] studied the tensile properties of post-fire tensile properties of S235JR structural steels. They stated that a temperature exposure of 600 °C or above may cause a decrease in strength. Kang et al. [ 8 ] explored the mechanical and fracture behavior of Q460 steel grade after a fire situation. They found that the strength values began to decrease when the test samples were exposed to temperatures above 650 °C. Qiang et al. [ 9 ] conducted tensile tests on S460 (mild steel) and S690 (high strength steel) test coupons which were subjected to elevated temperatures of up to 1000 °C. These coupons were cooled to room temperature in air. It was observed that post fire examinations on HSSs resulted in differences compared to those in mild steel due to different mechanisms. Equations were developed to estimate the mechanical behaviors of HSSs after fire exposure. Qiang et al. [ 10 ] performed similar tests on S960 steel. Up to 600 °C, the tensile properties of S960 did not change. Chiew et al. [ 11 ] investigated the mechanical behavior of reheated, quenched, and tempered S690 steel under fire and post-fire conditions. No significant change was observed up to 400 °C, but the strength significantly decreased after 600 °C. Chen et al. [ 12 ] examined HSS (approximately equivalent to S690Q) and mild steel up to 1000 °C. The results showed that both steels exhibited similar behavior in terms of reduction factors when the temperature range was up to 540 °C. Zeybek et al. [ 13 ] studied the post-fire mechanical behavior of S700MC high strength steels. Their results indicated that the strength and stiffness of most test samples remained largely unaffected until the temperature reached 600 °C. However, the behavior of S700MC is significantly affected when the temperature exceeds 600 °C. It has been observed that after exposure to elevated temperatures (600 °C and higher), the strength values decreased, while the ductility increased. Current design codes such as the American, Australian, British, and European standards were utilized to compare the outcomes of HSS subjected to elevated temperature. The comparative results showed that the current codes conservatively estimate yield strengths up to 1000 °C. Wang et al. [ 14 ] investigated the post fire performance of Q460 steels which were subjected to temperatures up to 900 °C, considering two different cooling methods (air cooling and water cooling). It has been reported that tensile properties decreased significantly after 600 °C. Heidarpour et al. [ 15 ] proposed equations to predict the yield and ultimate strengths on UHSS coupons which were subjected to elevated temperatures of up to 600 °C. It was reported that existing equations given by the Australian and American standards cannot be utilized to predict the tensile properties of UHSS. It is known that the ductility of HSS and UHSS is lower than that of mild steel, and design codes require minimum ductility levels for the plastic analysis method; therefore, those methods cannot be applicable for HSS and UHSS. Recently, Zeybek et al. (2024) have developed predictive equations to estimate changes in the mechanical behavior of HSS after fire exposure. Furthermore, some researchers have focused on the response of UHSSs after exposure to fire. Azhari et al. [ 16 ] investigated the fire and post-fire performance of UHSS. The test samples were subjected to elevated temperatures up to 600 °C. The tests were performed both under temperature and after cooling. It was reported that unlike UHSS, no significant strength reduction was observed in mild steel and HSS when subjected to elevated temperatures of up to 600 °C. Azhari et al. [ 17 ] studied the effects of different cooling methods such as water-quenching and air cooling on UHSS after fire up to a temperature of 900 °C. The strength of the samples subjected to air cooling after high temperatures above 700 °C was significantly reduced. The strength capacities were higher when the water quenching was applied. The results were different when these methods were applied to HSS and mild steel. The strength reduction in HSS due to fire was low when compared to UHSS. Both cooling methods yielded almost similar results. For mild steel cases, the water quenching method increased the ultimate strength capacity for the samples subject to high temperatures above 700 °C. Shi et al. [ 18 ] tested UHSS of cold formed Q1100 at various elevated temperatures up to 500 °C. Significant reduction in strength was observed when the temperatures were 500 °C. Predictive equations and a two-stage constitutive model were proposed and validated to describe the mechanical behavior of Q1100 UHSS accurately.

Luo et al. [ 19 ] investigated UHSS of cold formed Q1200 at various elevated temperatures. After a temperature of 200 °C, the capacity started to decrease significantly and more than 60% reduction was observed at 500 °C temperature.

It is certain that the microstructural changes occurring as a result of exposure to heat in any steel grade are not independent of its composition. The studies mentioned above clearly indicate that relatively short-term temperature exposures up until what is known as the eutectoid temperature (A1), i.e. 723 °C for mild steels, do not produce a significant effect on the mechanical properties. The reason is that such temperature levels do not cause any phase transformations in steels, but only microstructural coarsening. If exposure times were sufficiently prolonged, the effects on properties would also be readily noticeable. Exposure to temperatures above this threshold is bound to create phase transformations that would strongly influence the final properties. It should be borne in mind that the A 1  temperature, as well as two other critical temperatures defining a ferrite+austenite two-phase region, namely A 2  and A 3  temperatures, are composition dependent. Furthermore, another composition-dependent temperature exists —known as the Ms (martensite start) temperature — which renders the cooling rate from the maximum temperature attained during heat treatment or fire a critical factor. In addition, another complicating aspect, i.e. elemental partitioning (especially for a fast diffusing atom such as carbon) during the time elapsed at the exposed temperatures between the A2 and A3 phase boundaries of the equilibrium phase diagram of any steel, has to be considered if and when a mathematical approach is to be constructed for the prediction of mechanical properties following heat exposures. Moreover, cooling the steels after elevated temperatures can also generate residual stresses [ 16 ,  20 ,  21 ] depending on the steel grades and section thickness even if no phase transformation takes place. Therefore, predictive approaches so far can be said to remain empirical at best. It is also reasonable to assert that any such effort must be considered or used cautiously.

While substantial progress has been made in understanding the post-fire response of structural UHSS, design-oriented knowledge for wear-resistant steels remains limited, particularly under realistic cooling scenarios relevant to firefighting and industrial fires. Given their different alloying philosophies and microstructural stability, extrapolating existing UHSS degradation models is not justified. Accordingly, this study provides the first comprehensive post-fire dataset and predictive framework for Miilux 450, contributing new material-specific knowledge for post-fire evaluation of wear-resistant steels. This aim is important because WRSs—such as Miilux 450, a commercial ultra-high-strength grade with 400–480 HBW hardness and roughly 1,100 MPa yield strength—are increasingly used in heavily loaded mining and earthmoving equipment where fire or localized overheating is a realistic risk. Despite their widespread application, the post-fire performance of Miilux 450 and similar steels is largely unknown, especially regarding how different cooling methods representative of real fire scenarios affect their mechanical properties and microstructure. To address this need, the present study examines Miilux 450 after exposure to temperatures up to 1000 °C followed by air cooling (AC), water cooling (WC), or CO₂ fire-extinguisher cooling (CFE), evaluating residual strength, stiffness, hardness, and microstructural evolution to support post-fire reuse decisions and future performance-based design recommendations for WRSs.

sections.heading: Experimental Program
paragraphs: The material investigated in this study was Miilux 450 wear-resistant steel supplied in 6 mm thick plates. Three different cooling techniques were considered: air, water and CO₂ fire extinguisher cooling. Thus, the experimental investigation comprised of two main stages, i.e. identifying mechanical properties and microstructural characterization.

sections.heading: Test Materials
paragraphs: The test specimens shown were cut from steel plates having 6 mm thickness. Three different types of specimens were considered for mechanical and microstructural characterization. The sample type shown in Fig.  1 .a was used for tensile test specimens. Figure  1 .b illustrates the sample size employed to measure the modulus of elasticity by using the Resonant Frequency Damping Analyser (RFDA) system. Figure  1 .c shows the sample for the metallographic preparation and inspection. The nominal chemical composition provided by the manufacturer is listed in Table  1  (wt%), balance Fe.
Fig. 1 Geometry of specimens used for  a  tensile testing,  b  RFDA modulus measurement, and  c  metallographic analysis
Table 1 Chemical composition of high strength Miilux 450 steel C Mn Si P S B Cu Cr Ni Mo V 0.20 0.999 0.238 0.008 0.003 0.003 0.009 0.627 0.384 0.212 0.006

Miilux 450 is a wear-resistant steel grade produced by Miilux Oy. The plates are supplied in accordance with dimensional tolerances follow European standards EN 10,029 and inspection certificates are issued according to EN 10,204 (3.1).

Miilux 450 steel is initially produced in slab form through continuous casting and followed by hot rolling to the desired thickness. The hot-rolled plates are then heat-treated to achieve the final mechanical properties required for wear resistance. Applied heat treatment consists of two main stages: first, to obtain a homogeneous austenitic microstructure, the steel is heated to austenitization temperature. Following this, plates undergo a controlled water quenching process, in which rapid cooling promotes the martensitic transformation.

sections.heading: Heating and Cooling of Test Materials
paragraphs: Tensile test samples were exposed to designated elevated temperatures before testing. Thermal exposure tests were carried out using a PROTHERM laboratory muffle furnace (Fig.  2 ) to heat the specimens to the target temperatures prior to the prescribed holding and cooling procedures. As mentioned earlier, seven levels for elevated temperatures, i.e., from 400 °C up to 1000 °C (400 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C and 1000 °C) were chosen. The complete time–temperature history (heating, 30 min holding, and subsequent cooling) applied to the furnace and specimens is summarized in Fig.  3 . The figure presents the common heating/holding protocol and the distinct cooling regimes for AC, CFE, and WC, enabling direct comparison of thermal histories across all exposure temperatures. The heating rate was set to 10 °C/min to ensure a controlled and repeatable thermal history for all specimens and to remain consistent with commonly adopted protocols in post-fire coupon investigations of high-strength steels. Similar heating rates have been reported in post-fire experimental studies to provide stable and reproducible thermal conditioning for residual property evaluation [ 22 ]. All specimens were subjected to a uniform heating protocol with a fixed 30 min. holding duration at the target temperature to ensure consistent thermal exposure prior to cooling. Although the duration at θmax (i.e., soaking time) and the heating rate can influence microstructural evolution and residual strength, these parameters were intentionally kept constant in this study to isolate the effect of cooling conditions. The selected holding duration is consistent with typical post-fire experimental programs and provides a representative thermal exposure for evaluating residual mechanical behavior.
Fig. 2 PROTHERM laboratory muffle furnace used for thermal exposure tests
Fig. 3 Time–temperature history of furnace heating/holding and subsequent specimen cooling under different cooling conditions

The test samples shown in Fig.  4  were heated from room temperature to the holding temperatures given above. The tensile test specimens, the RFDA samples to measure the modulus of elasticity and the samples for microstructural evaluation were subjected to specific heating and cooling cycles before testing. All heat-treated samples were held in the furnace for 30 min at the chosen maximum temperature to ensure a uniform temperature distribution in the test samples. In order to assess the effect of the cooling rate on the mechanical and micro-structural behavior, test samples were cooled with 3 different cooling techniques- cooling in air (AC) as the slowest cooling rate, cooling in water (WC) as the fastest, and the CO2 fire extinguisher (CFE) as an intermediate cooling rate were considered.
Fig. 4 Tensile test specimens after exposure to elevated temperatures and different cooling methods (AC, WC, CFE)

After reaching the designated exposure temperature and completing the holding period, specimens were subjected to three cooling conditions. For air cooling (AC), specimens were removed from the furnace and allowed to cool naturally in still laboratory air until room temperature, representing slow cooling conditions. For water cooling (WC), specimens were immediately removed from the furnace and fully immersed in a water bath at ambient temperature (approximately 20–25 °C) and kept submerged until thermal equilibrium with room temperature was achieved. This approach is widely used in post-fire steel studies to simulate rapid cooling associated with firefighting water applications and to assess quench-sensitive behavior. Air- and water-cooling protocols are commonly used in post-fire investigations to represent slow and rapid cooling scenarios [ 14 ,  17 ]. In addition, CO₂ fire-extinguisher cooling (CFE) was introduced as an intermediate cooling condition. In this case, specimens were exposed to continuous CO₂ discharge immediately after furnace removal, providing a moderate cooling rate between air cooling and water quenching and better representing realistic firefighting practices. The noticeable color changes in Fig.  4  were attributed to varying levels of surface oxidation.

sections.heading: Tensile Testing of Specimens
paragraphs: Figure  4  indicates the Miilux 450 wear-resistant steel tensile specimens used in the post-fire mechanical investigation. As illustrated in Fig.  3 , the specimens were subjected to elevated temperatures ranging from room temperature (RT) to 1000 °C, and each was subsequently cooled using one of three methods: air cooling (AC), water cooling (WC), or CO₂ fire-extinguisher cooling (CFE). Tensile tests, on a total of 22 specimens machined out according to DIN 50125:2009-07, were conducted at room temperature.

Tensile tests were performed at room temperature using a Zwick/Roell Z250 testing machine with a staged rate-control procedure. A representative photograph of the test configuration, including the mounted specimen and grip arrangement, is provided in Fig.  5 . The same gripping and alignment procedure was applied consistently to all tests to ensure repeatable boundary conditions. A pre-load of 20 N was applied to ensure proper specimen seating. The initial loading stage was conducted under stress-rate control using a stress rate of 6 MPa/s for both the elastic and yield-parameter determination segments. This stress-rate level falls within the recommended range specified in ISO 6892-1 (6–60 MPa/s for metallic materials with modulus of elasticity ≥ 150 GPa), ensuring standardized quasi-static tensile testing conditions [ 23 ]. After yielding, the test was continued under strain-rate control, using a strain rate of 0.001 s⁻¹ in the yield range and 0.002 s⁻¹ for the subsequent loading stage up to failure. The same loading protocol was applied to all specimens to ensure reliable comparison of post-fire mechanical properties across temperatures and cooling conditions.
Fig. 5 Specimen gripping arrangement in the Zwick/Roell Z250 universal testing machine, showing the alignment and clamping of the tensile coupon between the upper and lower jaws

sections.heading: Microstructural Characteristics of Miilux 450 Steels
paragraphs: The changes in the microstructural characteristics of these specimens after heating and cooling cycles replicating fire exposure should also be examined for the Fitness-for-Service (FFS) assessment. The Hardness test is important for evaluating the material strength after a fire scenario. Using the Duroline-M Microhardness Tester, micro hardness values of test samples were measured.

The metallographic samples were prepared through a standard methodology of mounting, grinding (SiC papers of decreasing grit sizes), polishing with colloidal silica, and finally etching with Nital (2% nitric acid in ethanol). The imaging of all microstructures was done using SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy) operated at 15 kV and employing an SE (secondary electron) detector. Subsequently, etched samples were prepared for scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis. In order to save space, microstructural images have been given here only for the selected most critical heat treatment temperatures, namely room temperature (RT-20 °C), 600 °C, 800 °C and 1000 °C, and for 3 different cooling regimes from those temperatures.

sections.heading: Stress–Strain Relationships
paragraphs: The tensile tests conducted following the heat-treatment cycles that were concluded via different cooling rates resulted in the stress-strain curves given in Figs.  6 ,  7  and  8 . Strains in Figs.  6 ,  7  and  8  were measured using a contact extensometer mounted on the gauge length (Fig.  5 ). Due to strain localization after the onset of necking, the reported fracture strain represents an apparent engineering value; however, this does not affect the primary mechanical parameters of interest in this study (Fy, Fu, and E), which are derived from the pre-necking portion of the response.
Fig. 6 Stress-strain curves of Miilux 450 steel for AC
Fig. 7 Stress-strain curves of Miilux 450 steel for WC
Fig. 8 Stress-strain curves of Miilux 450 steel for CFE

As shown in Figs.  6 ,  7  and  8 , the post fire mechanical behavior of the test samples was different when compared to that of the original steel at room temperature for each of the cooling rates employed. The original steel and most of the specimens after exposure to the replicated fire did not show any clear yield point or yield plateau region. Mechanical properties such as the modulus of elasticity ( E ), 0.2% yield stress or strength (σ 0.2 ), stress at 0.5% strain (σ 0.5 ), stress at 1.5% strain (σ 1.5 ), stress at 2.0% strain (σ 2.0 ) and ultimate tensile strength (σ u ) were identified using the stress-strain curves of the test specimens. Definitions of the above-mentioned characteristic strength and corresponding strain values have been given in Fig.  9 .
Fig. 9 Symbols for identifying mechanical properties

After tensile testing, failure modes for the test specimens have been shown in Fig.  10 . The fracture modes of the tensile specimens were examined in relation to the temperature to which they were exposed and the cooling method applied. At room temperature and across all temperature levels, distinct necking behavior was observed in the specimens, indicating that the ductile fracture mechanism was maintained under all experimental conditions. Although significant changes in strength parameters were observed with increasing temperature, no distinct difference emerged in the general character of the fracture behavior. The necking behavior persisted in all specimens, and no transition to brittle fracture behavior was observed. Although some local differences were observed among the cooling methods (particularly a tendency toward sharper localization in the WC specimens), this did not alter the general fracture mechanism. The specimens cooled in air (AC) and by CO₂ fire extinguisher (CFE) maintained more distributed deformation patterns, although with reduced elongation compared to the original material. These observations confirm that while WC enhances strength recovery at high temperatures, it simultaneously reduces deformation capacity, leading to a strength–ductility trade-off.
Fig. 10 Failure modes of tensile specimens after different thermal exposures and cooling methods, showing necking and fracture characteristics

sections.heading: Yield Strengths
paragraphs: The yield strength is an important indicator for the onset of permanent deformation or change in material shape under applied stress. After tensile testing of the coupon specimens, yield strength values were identified. As already mentioned, since the stress-strain curves provide no clear yield plateau, proof stress values were employed. Thus the yield strength values at different strain values such as (σ 0.2 ) T , (σ 0.5 ) T , (σ 1.5 ) T  and (σ 2.0 ) T  were obtained from the stress-strain curves.

The yield strength values of the above-mentioned samples after exposure to fire-replicating cycles were compared with the values of the test samples without heat treatment (at ambient temperature). The normalized values for each of the cooling methods were plotted as a function of temperature. Thus, changes in the yield strength levels at different strain values of the test specimens after exposure to elevated temperatures have been shown in Figs.  11 ,  12 ,  13  and  14 .
Fig. 11 Changes in the (σ 0.2 ) T  of Miilux 450 steel test specimens for three cooling methods and the proposed model
Fig. 12 Changes in the (σ 0.5 ) T  of Miilux 450 steel test specimens for three cooling methods and the proposed model
Fig. 13 Changes in the (σ 1.5 ) T  of Miilux 450 steel test specimens for three cooling methods and the proposed model
Fig. 14 Changes in the (σ 2.0 ) T  of Miilux 450 steel test specimens for three cooling methods and the proposed model

Figures  11 ,  12 ,  13  and  14  indicate that as the exposed temperatures increased until 700 °C, yield strength values decreased for the three different cooling techniques. The reduction in yield strength values reached 60%. The effect of cooling techniques on yield strength values of the Miilux 450 steel was minor. However, heat treatment and cooling methods after 700 °C provide noticeable influence on test specimens. While a small increase was observed in yield strength for the cases AC and CFE, there was a significant increase in the yield value of the specimens after WC. Subsequently, a small decrease was observed for all three cooling cases. In all cases, the original yield strength of the material appeared to be higher. This observation can be accounted for possibly by considering the carbon losses from the samples and microstructural coarsening as compared to the original plate material, which was a hot deformation product. Thus, the observed decrease in these figures (Figs.  11 ,  12 ,  13  and  14 ) until about 700 °C has been attributed to microstructural coarsening. However, the following relative increase can be explained by the presence of phase transformations and the resulting austenite to martensite transformation.

As shown in Fig.  15 , in accordance with the 700 °C condition, a sharp increase in tensile strength is observed at 800 °C for the water-cooled specimens. This behavior is associated with the phase transformation occurring above the eutectoid temperature (A₁). At 700 °C, which is below the A₁ temperature, no austenite formation occurs, and the microstructural evolution is primarily governed by the coarsening of the existing phases, depending on the cooling rate. Consequently, all cooling methods yield nearly identical tensile properties at this temperature.
Fig. 15 Changes in the (σ u ) T  of Miilux 450 steel test specimens for three cooling methods and proposed model

In contrast, at 800 °C the material lies within the intercritical region, resulting in partial austenite formation. Upon rapid water cooling, the austenite phase transform into martensite, leading to a hardening effect and an increase in tensile strength compared to the 700 °C condition. However, in the case of AC and CFE, the slower cooling rates promote the formation of diffusional transformation products and resulting in lower tensile strength than WC specimens. These observations are consistent with the SEM which reveal evidence of newly formed martensitic regions in the 800 °C WC condition.

sections.heading: Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS)
paragraphs: UTS is a crucial material parameter and it refers to the maximum stress that a material can resist before rupture. Changes in ultimate strength values can be found by considering the ratio of the tensile strength of the test specimen after cooling ((σ u ) T ) to that of the original material at room temperature ((σ u ) AT ). The normalized values ((σ u ) T /(σ u ) AT ) for each cooling method were plotted as a function of temperature. UTS values obtained from the stress-strain curves have been compared with those reported in the literature in Fig.  15 .

As observed in the changes of yield strength values, Fig.  15  indicates that as the temperature increases until 700 °C, ultimate tensile strength values decrease for the three different cooling techniques. The reduction in ultimate strength values reached 55% for the WC case. The effect of cooling techniques on the ultimate tensile strength values of Miilux 450 steel was minor. However, the heat treatment and cooling method after 700 °C provides noticeable influence on the test specimens. While a small increase was observed in yield strength for the cases AC and CFE, there was a significant increase in the yield value of the specimens after WC. Thereafter, a small decrease was observed in the three cooling cases. The decrease until about 700 °C and the following increase in the case of samples treated at higher temperatures can again be explained as expressed in the discussion for Figs.  11 ,  12 ,  13  and  14  above.

sections.heading: Modulus of Elasticity
paragraphs: The modulus of elasticity is an indicator of the stiffness of the material. Rectangular test specimens based on ASTM E1876-15 were prepared to measure the elastic modulus via the Resonance Frequency and Damping Analysis (RFDA) technique (see Fig.  16 ). RFDA is a non-destructive testing technique designed to assess the dynamic elastic properties of materials, particularly the dynamic Young’s modulus. In this method, the rectangular sample is mechanically excited, usually by tapping or through an actuator, and its natural resonance frequencies are recorded using a microphone or vibration sensor. These frequencies are then used to calculate mechanical properties such as the dynamic Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio. The dynamic Young’s modulus is specifically derived from the resonance frequency of the specimen when it vibrates in either the flexural or longitudinal modes. Unlike the static modulus obtained through tensile testing, the dynamic modulus tends to be slightly lower—often about 5%—because it reflects the response of the material under the effect of local heat generated by elastic deformation, whereas, for example, a tensile test allows sufficient time for this heat to be dissipated. This method is a fast, non-destructive technique that requires minimal sample preparation and is highly sensitive to small changes in material properties. In order to determine the changes in the modulus of elasticity values of the samples after heat treatment cycles, (( E ) T ) values were normalized with those of the original material at room temperature (( E ) T /( E ) AT ). The normalized values were then plotted as a function of temperature. Thus, changes in the modulus of elasticity values of test specimens after exposure to elevated temperatures have been shown in Fig.  17 .
Fig. 16 RFDA test set up
Fig. 17 Changes in the elastic modulus of ultra-high strength Miilux 450 steel test specimens for the three cooling methods and the proposed model

Figure  17  indicates that there was no significant reduction in the modulus of elasticity values of test specimens until 700 °C. As shown in Fig.  17 , the reduction in elastic modulus is more pronounced for temperatures higher than 700 °C. The highest measured reduction was 12% when the heating temperature reached 1000 °C. Furthermore, the effect of the cooling method on the change in elastic modulus is negligible. The noticeable decline in the elastic modulus following 600 °C for all samples was attributed to microstructural changes, i.e. to a minor coarsening effect until about 700 °C. The following continuing minor decrease possibly was the result of an interplay between two opposing effects, i.e. the generation of some martensite that apparently did not overcome those effects that lower the elastic modulus, such as soft ferrite with extremely low dislocation density, and tempering effects on the martensitic portions during cooling to room temperature even in the case of water quenching.

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: Hardness refers to material resistance to the applied force without deformation. Thus, it can provide an important input for fitness-for-service investigations. In microstructure analysis, changes in hardness of Miilux 450 steel were explored. To pursue this goal, the ratio of hardness value of test specimens after exposure to elevated temperatures to that of the test specimen at ambient temperature was calculated and plotted as a function of temperature in Fig.  18 .
Fig. 18 Changes in the ( H v ) T  of Miilux 450 steel test specimens for three cooling methods and proposed model

As can be seen from Fig.  18 , a trend similar to the yield and ultimate strengths given in Figs.  11 ,  12 ,  13  and  14  and  15  was observed. The hardness value decreased when the test samples were heated up to 700 °C. However, these values start to increase when the temperature value exceeds 700 °C. This increase is more pronounced for the samples with WC. Since hardness is a mechanical property that changes in accordance with strength, the explanations for the observed changes can be none other than those already given to account for the changes in strength in the paragraphs above.

The interaction diagram between temperature, hardness, and ultimate tensile strength is illustrated in the 3D figure (see Fig.  19 ). Naturally, a strong positive correlation between these parameters over the whole range of tested cooling methods and temperatures was detected. Up to 700 °C, all cooling methods consistently demonstrated a reduction in both hardness and ultimate strength. In general, the samples with higher hardness values also exhibited higher ultimate tensile strength. The general trends clearly diverge at temperatures above 700 °C. Due to faster quenching, the samples with WC exhibited a noticeable recovery in hardness and ultimate strength, whereas the samples with AC and CFE only show slight increases. Overall, the samples with WC continuously maintain higher ultimate strength and hardness levels at the highest test temperatures compared with those of the samples with AC and CFE. Across the entire temperature range, a strong correlation between UTS and hardness is observed. This indicates that the changes in hardness after fire exposure closely mirror variations in tensile performance.
Fig. 19 Interaction diagram between ultimate tensile strength and hardness

sections.heading: SEM Analysis
paragraphs: In this study, the basic Fe–C phase diagram is considered as a reference, and all microstructural examinations and interpretations have been given accordingly. It should be noted that the addition of alloying elements can significantly alter the position of phase transformation temperatures, i.e., modify the phase fields by shifting their boundaries. However, for the purpose of this study, the Fe–C diagram provides a reliable framework for interpretation.

The microstructure of the steel at room temperature is shown in Fig.  20  labelled with RT, revealing a ferrite plus pearlite structure which can be characterized by its lamellar structure. This structure serves as a baseline for comparing the microstructures of other samples subjected to different heating-cooling cycles. The microstructure of the sample 600 A in Fig.  20  belongs to a sample cooled from 600 °C in air. This temperature is below the eutectoid temperature in the Fe–C phase diagram, where the microstructure consists of pearlite and ferrite. Heating the sample to this temperature followed by slow cooling does not induce a phase transformation. In extreme cases where the duration of stay at this temperature is too long, this heat treatment can cause grain coarsening in the ferritic grains and spheroidization in the pearlite. However, due to the short holding time at this temperature and low diffusion rates, grain coarsening in ferrite was not noticeable and no spheroidization was observed when compared to the original microstructure at room temperature. Grain coarsening in ferrite, if any, is noticeable under slower cooling conditions. Specifically, for samples heat treated at 600 °C, CFE cooling was observed to have coarsened the grain size as compared to that at room temperature due to the prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures during slow cooling (See Fig.  21 ).
Fig. 20 SE SEM micrograph of room temperature sample and air-cooled sample from 600 °C
Fig. 21 SEM micrograph of sample cooled from 600 °C  a  with CFE and  b  via water quenching

A water-quenched sample from 800 °C (Fig.  22 ) reveals a mixed microstructure consisting of martensite and ferrite. It should also be borne in mind that due to the incomplete nature of martensitic transformation, the austenitic constituent must also involve some untransformed austenitic portion, that is ‘retained austenite’. Given the carbon content of 0.2 wt%, the steel falls within the hypoeutectoid range, and at 800 °C, the heat treatment lies within the two-phase region (intercritical range) (α + γ) of the Fe–C phase diagram. After heating to 800 °C, the holding time influences the amount of austenite that will form. As the isothermal holding temperature and time increase, the amount of austenite will increase as well. This amount will be below the equilibrium amount of austenite that can form at the holding temperature.
Fig. 22 SEM micrograph of sample cooled from 800 °C with air and CFE

The holding time in the intercritical region (ferrite+austenite) will influence the carbon partitioning between ferrite and austenite as well. This partitioning results in austenite enriching in carbon relative to ferrite and also to the original steel composition, since it is an austenite stabilizing element. The austenite which will form by holding at 800 °C will therefore involve the majority of the carbon of the original steel. This relatively high carbon austenite compared to the original steel will transform either into the equilibrium constituents or into martensite depending on the cooling rate. At high cooling rates, the water quenched sample from 800 °C would form martensite with its austenitic portion that formed during isothermal holding. This martensite, in fact, would have greater hardness compared to the one which would form after quenching from an isothermal holding-temperature that falls into the fully austenitic phase field in the Fe-C equilibrium diagram. This is so because the carbon content of austenite would expectedly be lower when the entire structure is composed of austenite, as in the fully austenitic structure compared to the partially austenitic structure that contains the almost entire carbon content of the original composition. The higher carbon content martensitic phase would likely have a higher dislocation density as well (See Fig.  23 ).
Fig. 23 SEM micrograph of samples water cooled from 800 degrees and air cooled from 1000 degrees

This hard and brittle martensitic constituent significantly increases the strength and hardness of the material, though at the expense of ductility. The coexistence of ferrite plus martensite produces a microstructure that achieves a balance between strength, contributed by martensite, and ductility, provided by ferrite.

The microstructure of the air-cooled sample from 1000 °C consists of pearlite, exhibiting a finer pearlitic-nodular size compared to the CFE-cooled sample (see Fig.  24 ). This refinement is attributed to the faster cooling rate of air cooling, which prevents the growth of pearlitic nodules. In contrast, the microstructure of the sample subjected to quenching from the austenitic range (1000 W) shows a martensitic morphology. Due to the absence of elemental partitioning in the fully austenitic region, the entire carbon content now resides in a greater amount of austenite. Thus, the resulting martensite contains less carbon relative to the martensite of the 800 W sample. Consequently, the martensite formed after the 1000 W treatment exhibits relatively lower hardness compared to the martensite obtained by quenching, following holding at the intercritical temperature (See Figs.  15  and  18 ).
Fig. 24 The SEM micrograph samples cooled from 1000 degrees with CFE and water

sections.heading: Comparison with Literature Studies and Proposed Predictive Equations
paragraphs: There is almost no comprehensive research addressing the behavior of wear-resistant ultra-high-strength steels after exposure to fire. Existing studies primarily focus on conventional structural steels, high-strength steels (HSS), and a limited selection of ultra-high-strength steels (UHSS), but they rarely include commercial wear-plate grades such as Miilux or Hardox. Moreover, investigations on the post-fire mechanical properties of UHSS with nominal yield strengths exceeding 960 MPa are scarce, and the available data typically cover only a small range of temperatures or do not incorporate the effects of different cooling conditions. For meaningful comparisons, therefore, only UHSS grades with nominal yield strengths above 960 MPa were considered in this study. This approach allows the post-fire behavior of Miilux 450 to be evaluated in the context of steels with broadly similar strength levels, while also highlighting the absence of systematic data for wear-resistant steels in available fire engineering literature. In consequence, the mechanical characteristics acquired from these researchers were used to evaluate the experimental test outcomes of this investigation and develop predictive equations of the mechanical properties of UHSS after exposure to fire.

Motivated by this gap, the mechanical characteristics reported in previous UHSS studies were used to benchmark the experimental findings obtained in the present work and to assist in developing predictive equations for the post-fire mechanical properties of UHSS. Among these, Azhari and her research team [ 16 ,  17 ,  24 ] performed notable experimental investigations on Grade 1200 UHSS, examining its behavior up to 800 °C under air and water cooling. Accordingly, the test data presented by Azhari et al. [ 16 ,  17 ,  24 ] were incorporated into the comparative assessment to support the formulation of the proposed predictive equations.
Figures  8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11  and  12  compare the outcome of this study and the mechanical characteristics of UHSSs in the literature as a function of temperature.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, the microstructure and mechanical properties of the wear-resistant Miilux 450 steels subjected to elevated temperatures were investigated considering three different cooling methods, namely, Air Cooling [AC], Water Cooling [WC] and Fire Extinguisher Cooling [CFE]. This investigation consists of two parts, i.e., the experimental and parametric methods. In the experimental part, tensile tests were conducted to identify post-fire mechanical properties such as hardness, yield strength values at different strains, the ultimate tensile strength and the modulus of elasticity. Moreover, micro-structure examination was conducted using optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The results obtained can be summarized as follows.

Up to 700 °C, the yield strength, ultimate strength and hardness decreased significantly regardless of cooling methods. Above 700 °C, mechanical recovery was observed in all cooling methods. However, the mechanical recovery was significantly higher in the samples with WC compared to other cooling methods. The modulus of elasticity remained almost stable up to 700 °C. Above 700 °C, a slightly higher reduction in modulus of elasticity was detected regardless of the cooling method. Hardness and ultimate strength demonstrated strong correlation for the tested temperature range. Overall, the most pronounced property recovery is detected in the cooling method of WC due to rapid quenching, whereas AC and CFE result in comparatively limited restoration of mechanical properties. The SEM examinations revealed that microstructural changes occurred in the original steel following the fire-replicating heat treatment cycles. The proposed predictive equations provide temperature and cooling method dependent relationships for estimating post-fire mechanical performance which strongly parallel the observed trends.
